entries.title: OPM Director Scott Kupor Publicly Touted Robinhood. He’s Also an Investor.
entries.summary: A Kupor spokesperson said government ethics officials didn’t require him to divest his investment in the financial services company.
entries.content:
In December, U.S. Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor highlighted a partnership between financial services company Robinhood Markets Inc. and the Trump administration that temporarily places skilled private-sector tech workers in federal government jobs.

“We’re doing this in partnership with about 25 of the tech companies that you all know and love — so, you know, Coinbase, Robinhood, Databricks, Snowflake, NVIDIA, xAI, OpenAI,” Kupor told technology news show TBPN in explaining the Trump administration’s “US Tech Force” initiative.

Screenshot 2026-07-30 at 8.05.51 PM.png (726x768, AR: 0.95)What Kupor didn’t say: He has maintained massive personal financial interests in Robinhood. And last month, the OPM director exercised stock call options and sold seven figures worth of his Robinhood shares, according to new federal ethics records reviewed by NOTUS.

Kupor’s Robinhood stock sales on June 18 are together worth between $1.7 million and $3.5 million, a disclosure document filed with the Office of Government Ethics indicates.

They came on a day when Robinhood’s stock price closed at $108.15 per share — up significantly from the year-to-date low closing price of $65.16 on March 30.

In recent days, Robinhood stock has generally traded between $85 and $95 per share.

Robinhood has other ties to President Donald Trump’s administration.

Kupor and Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev are both quoted in a press release detailing the Tech Force initiative. Robinhood is meanwhile working with the Treasury Department to launch and maintain an app for the government’s new Trump Accounts program, which aims to provide children with tax-deferred investment accounts. And Robinhood offered prediction market contracts on matters involving the federal government, including government shutdowns, which OPM monitors.

Kupor also reported exercising stock call options and selling between $3 million and $12 million worth of stock in Okta Inc. on June 18, according to ethics records. Okta, an identity verification tech company, is a federal government contractor.

In an ethics agreement Kupor signed last year prior to his Senate confirmation, he agreed to take steps to “avoid any actual or apparent conflict of interest” and divest of dozens of personal investments. He also resigned from various corporate posts and positions.

In a statement to NOTUS, OPM spokesperson McLaurine Pinover said Kupor “went through a full financial review with [the Office of Government Ethics] prior to his confirmation hearing and agreed to all divestitures and recusals proposed by OGE. Neither Okta nor Robinhood were suggested by OGE as divestitures since OPM has no financial relationship with either company.”

The OGE declined to comment on Kupor’s personal investments.

The agency’s published “conflicts of interest considerations” guidance states that “an employee who owns stock options is prohibited from participating personally and substantially in any particular matter that the employee knows would have a direct and predictable effect on the financial interests of the issuer of the underlying security.”

Walter Shaub, who served as director of the Office of Government Ethics from 2013 to 2017, said Trump has set an “anything goes” standard for how his top lieutenants can invest their personal assets. The president reported thousands of stock and bond trades during the past year and has routinely engaged in private crypto and other business ventures since returning to the White House in 2025.

“It has seemed to me that the president’s appointees are doing a whole lot of buying and selling investments. That’s not something you saw happening much in the past Democratic or Republican administrations,” Shaub said.

“The problem is that letting presidential appointees play the market is a recipe for disaster,” Shaub added. “There’s no way for the public to know which government decisions are made because they’ll be lucrative for administration officials instead of being made because they’re what’s best for the American people.”

In recent months, several top Trump administration officials have made notable personal financial trades or deals while serving in public office.

They include FBI Director Kash Patel, Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, Ambassador to Italy Tilman Fertitta, Federal Highway Administration Administrator Sean McMaster, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, Small Business Administration Administrator Kelly Loeffler, former U.S. Agency for Global Media leader Kari Lake, Department of Homeland Security Undersecretary Pedro Allende, Environmental Protection Agency Assistant Administrator Douglas Troutman and former Department of Health and Human Services general counsel Mike Stuart.

entries.title: Trump Announces Deal for ‘Complete Disarmament’ of Hamas
entries.summary: This agreement is a key step for the region to eventually be led by a new Palestinian government, the president said Thursday.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced on Thursday an agreement for the “complete disarmament” of Hamas militants in Gaza — what he called a “monumental step” toward ending conflict in the region.

Under the agreement — another phase of a ceasefire plan he unveiled last fall — Israeli forces will withdraw as Hamas completes the disarmament process, Trump wrote on Truth Social. He said Palestinians would work closely with the Board of Peace, which was established in January to oversee implementation of the peace plan, in hopes of moving toward “Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government.”

Israel and Hamas have not commented on the announcement, and it remains unclear if or how either party plans to honor the disarmament. The U.S. has been in close coordination with Israel “every step of the way,” administration and Board of Peace officials said Thursday, though Israel remains “very skeptical that Hamas will disarm.”

In January, the Trump administration created the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, a transitional leadership body that calls itself a “technocratic, and apolitical Palestinian committee.” This agreement is a key step for the region to eventually be led by a new Palestinian government, which Trump says will work closely with the Board of Peace.

“Hamas and factions will hand over their weapons to the NCAG and to the NCAG police forces, who will be responsible for collecting them, itemizing them and effectively controlling them,” the officials said.

The timetable for the phased withdrawal of Israeli forces still needs to be finalized, the officials said. The process of disarming smaller militia groups in Gaza, which are generally less structured and have more fragmented leadership, needs to happen before Hamas’ weapons can be fully decommissioned, the officials said.

“Our intention is to hold Israel to its commitments as well, and to make sure we can be a fair broker here,” the officials said.

Hamas and Israel agreed to the deployment of the International Stabilization Force, the United Nations-mandated peacekeeping body introduced through a U.S.-backed framework accepted last October. The troops, whose Gaza operations Israel approved this week, will train and work with a new Palestinian police force to help maintain security in the region while supporting the NCAG’s efforts to decommission weapons in Gaza.

Trump said the agreement honors both Israel and Gaza’s security concerns.

“Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks,” Trump wrote on Thursday.

Trump’s Board of Peace has faced criticism in the international community. The organization’s charter gives the president broad authority as chairman of the board.

“The Board of Peace has been authorized by the Security Council for its work on Gaza. Strictly for that,” United Nations spokesperson Farhan Haq told reporters in New York in January.

entries.title: Tech Companies Are Rejecting Trump’s Proposed ‘Woke’ AI Ban
entries.summary: The government’s proposed requirement for contractors’ AI systems to be “unbiased” are technically “infeasible,” businesses say.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is in the middle of finding out that it’s very hard — maybe even impossible — to regulate perceived “wokeness” in artificial intelligence.

The government’s main procurement agency is a year into trying to translate President Donald Trump’s ban on “woke” AI into contracting language, and technology companies are pouring out in opposition to what they’ve come up with.

The General Services Administration has formally proposed requiring companies to adhere to a broad list of “unbiased AI principles” in the systems they sell to the government, including “historical accuracy” and neutrality.

One trade group of software companies, including many government contractors, the Business Software Alliance, called the proposal “infeasible” in a comment submitted to the General Services Administration. Others called it an “impossible” standard.

The proposal could lead to reduced performance in AI systems, undermine developer safety practices and make it difficult for technology companies to contract with the government at a time when the Trump administration wants to ramp up AI adoption, lawyers, AI companies and AI experts say.

Under its draft guidance, the government would be able to test these systems for bias without disclosing how it’s doing so, and contractors would have to pay decommissioning costs if their contract is terminated as a result.

Contractors would also face potential legal exposure under the False Claims Act.

“That’s a huge penalty for something that I think is such a mushy framework,” Jessica Tillipman, associate dean for government procurement law studies at George Washington University, said of the efforts to ban “woke” AI.

“How, in a world in which your political viewpoint colors what you believe to be the truth … is that enforced in the contract?” she asked. “Maybe what’s considered truthful is determined by whoever is in power in that moment, right? I think that’s one of the harder things.”

This is the GSA’s second attempt at drafting contracting language for AI. The previous version required contractors to make “commercial efforts” to ensure that their systems comply with the administration’s principles.

The newer draft simply requires that systems be unbiased.

Large language models need to be “truthful in responding to user prompts seeking factual information or analysis,” the most recent draft reads.

“The LLM must prioritize historical accuracy, scientific inquiry, and objectivity and must acknowledge uncertainty where reliable information is incomplete or contradictory,” the proposal says. “The LLM must be a neutral, nonpartisan tool that does not manipulate responses in favor of ideological dogmas.”

Guaranteeing factual accuracy of AI systems is not technically possible, the Business Software Alliance says — “they are inherently probabilistic” — and being “nonpartisan” isn’t specific enough to be rendered technically, the group wrote.

“Compliance with the proposed clauses could result in reduced performance and lower accuracy, which could itself result in biased outcomes, subjecting the government to legal liability,” the Business Software Alliance’s comment reads.

The Information Technology Industry Council — another global tech trade association and advocacy group whose members include Google and OpenAI — is asking the administration to drop its requirement for “unbiased AI” altogether, Megan Petersen, the group’s counsel and senior vice president of public sector policy, told NOTUS.

“Without clear definitions and transparent compliance benchmarks, contractors will be held to an impossible performance standard,” Petersen said, noting that these requirements are also supposed to flow down throughout the LLM supply chain, which could further amplify this uncertainty.

“ITI is concerned that GSA’s language will discourage innovative commercial companies from doing business with the U.S. government altogether,” she said.

Joel Thayer, a senior fellow for AI and emerging technology policy at the America First Policy Institute, a right-wing think tank, told NOTUS that the government is “just laying out the ground rules ahead of time.”

“Sorry, but spare me,” he said when asked about the contractors’ concerns over the ambiguity of the proposed GSA language. “I don’t buy it at all. I think they totally understand what the contract means.”

“If I were to consult a textbook, would I get the same information that I would get from an AI?” he asked. “Or am I getting information that is being contextualized in some way and formed in a way that is giving me a conclusion that may be true, may not be true?”

Though, he said, where he will “credit” the companies, is that “there should be some more discovery on” how to enforce the government’s terms that AI systems are neutral.

Michael Tammero, a GSA spokesperson, told NOTUS in a statement that "GSA is in the process of establishing acquisition requirements to protect government data in LLM systems, and we welcome further stakeholder input on the rule” when asked about the concerns.

The deadline to submit comments is Aug. 3.

The requirement that contractors ensure that their AI systems are unbiased is tucked inside of a broader proposed rule on AI acquisition that the administration posted in June. If finalized, the contract clause would shape the terms under which the entire federal government buys AI.

The proposal follows the high-profile dispute between the Trump administration and the AI company Anthropic, which Trump called a “RADICAL LEFT, WOKE COMPANY” for its request during contract negotiations with the Pentagon that its systems not be used to power fully autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillance.

Trump ordered agencies to stop using the Anthropic in February, at which point the Pentagon quickly designated the company as a supply chain risk. Lawsuits over the dispute are ongoing.

Now, the GSA’s draft contracting language has the potential to affect the rest of the government’s contracting base.

In addition to applying to contracts the GSA maintains for government-wide use, the proposal would also likely become a template for other agencies, too, as they try to convert administration guidance banning “woke” AI models in the government into legal language, according to Tillipman.

Outside experts call it all a futile endeavor.

“This idea of building a system that’s ideologically neutral … has no scientific basis or sense whatsoever,” Suresh Venkatasubramanian, director of the Center for Technological Responsibility, Reimagination and Redesign who previously worked on AI policy for the Biden administration, said. “There is no such thing as unbiased AI.”

That may be the point, he said.

“The way these rules are set up is to create enough ambiguity and confusion so that the administration can exert power and control in whatever way they see without being able to get any pushback,” he said. “The goal is to dictate how these companies operate.”

Venkatasubramanian is also tracking a proposed policy statement that the Federal Trade Commission issued earlier this month, warning that AI companies could run afoul of the Federal Trade Commission Act’s ban on unfair or deceptive business practices by steering the outputs of their AI systems, even if it’s done to comply with a state law.

The FTC said that a company would “abuse consumer trust” if developers train AI systems to “correct what the developer believes are ‘historical injustices’” when the model responds to factual questions.

“What we're seeing here is a series of relatively unprecedented actions being taken by the current administration in an effort to impose their political ideology, viewpoints and objectives on AI developers through a range of policy-level levers at their disposal,” said Quinn Anex-Ries, a senior policy analyst at the Center for Democracy and Technology.

The result could shape consumer-facing AI, too. If developers have to change a system for the government to comply with the Trump administration’s contract terms for unbiased AI, they may not want to maintain a separate, consumer system, too, said Anex-Ries.

entries.title: D.C.’s Worst Landlord Is Its Housing Authority
entries.summary: The Department of Buildings fines the city’s bad landlords. None owe more than the DCHA.
entries.content:
D.C.’s beleaguered housing authority — which has faced leadership turnover, a cyberattack and a scathing audit this year — is the city’s worst offender when it comes to unresolved housing violations.

The District’s housing authority (DCHA) owes D.C.’s Department of Buildings (DOB) more than $2.2 million for over 2,500 unresolved violations across its properties, per a public DOB dashboard. Some violations date back to 2019.

The issue stems in part from the fact that the agency, which owns more than 8,500 public housing units, polices itself. Unlike private landlords who answer to DOB, by law, DOB cannot do more than issue fines to the housing authority.

“If someone calls us up, we’ll go out, we’ll inspect, we will see what’s broken, we’ll create a [notice of infraction], and we will provide it to DCHA. They are supposed to then fix it and tell us,” Keith Parsons, DOB’s director of strategic enforcement, told NOTUS. “There is really no ‘stick,’ by law.”

That the housing authority is the District’s worst offender doesn’t surprise Megan Browder, Legal Aid DC’s director for systemic advocacy and law reform.

“I think it is partially the size of the portfolio and also a systematic disregard for their mission,” Browder told NOTUS.

In 2022, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development found that DCHA was out of compliance with its annual inspection requirements, inspection outcomes weren’t monitored, and emergency work orders went uncompleted at night due to safety concerns. In 2020, D.C.’s attorney general sued the DCHA for endangering thousands of tenants across 10 of its properties.

D.C. has the country’s highest rates of rent nonpayment for low-income tax credit buildings, a fact landlords often point to as an explanation for their inability to make repairs. But DCHA doesn’t have that excuse, Browder said, as their properties are subsidized by the government.

“DCHA takes steps to fully abate any infraction within the abatement timeframe listed on the notice and provide proof of abatement to the DOB,” Alison Burdo, a DCHA spokesperson, told NOTUS in a statement. “There may be a delay in updates to DOB’s public database if further clarification between DCHA and DOB is needed.”

Some of the violations on the public dashboard are “associated with vacant units currently undergoing modernization or awaiting modernization pending sufficient funding,” Burdo said, and others are for properties DCHA doesn’t own or control but where the agency may have a long-term ground lease for redevelopment.

The housing authority is in the middle of a three-year “recovery plan” meant to improve the quality of its housing stock and improve work order systems, among other goals. The agency meets monthly with DOB to review any notices of infraction, Burdo said.

DHCA is far from the only landlord with an extensive list of outstanding violations. Per DOB’s dashboard, more than 84,500 housing violations, dating back to 2018, are currently unresolved, with more than $83 million in associated fines. More than 100 landlords owe at least $100,000 each.

Some of the violations — particularly those dating back years — are in active litigation, Parsons said. Others may have already been fixed, but either DOB is waiting for evidence of that abatement or associated fines are tied up in the department’s adjudication process.

That adjudication process is why it’s so hard to collect. It starts when DOB issues a notice of infraction after a property inspection, which may also carry a fine. There, the department runs into its first problem: the D.C. Council found in 2024 that over half of those infraction notices were sent to the incorrect address.

Once a landlord receives a notice, the department must take them through a monthslong appeal and adjudication process administered by the city’s Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) in order to collect any money.

“A landlord is entitled to due process,” Browder said. “That does take time, largely because there’s a big backlog at OAH.”

Because of that system, each year DOB receives just a fraction of the fines it assessed and abates less than half of violations. In the 2024 fiscal year, the department collected $2.6 million in fines, but referred $25 million more to the city’s collections unit.

Even as D.C. navigates a tight fiscal era, the DOB argues that the best outcome for the city is not necessarily collecting that $83 million.

“Success is making sure the problems are fixed, and the fines are a way to motivate the landlord to do it,” Parsons told NOTUS. “So, if we can get things fixed, that is our goal.”

In that spirit, and in line with the council’s recommendations from 2024, the department is shifting its approach. Instead of chasing down every penny owed, the department is trying to settle with landlords for less or no money in order to fix violations sooner. It has set a “very ambitious” goal of resolving 80% of emergency violations within 30 days, and 90 days for non-emergencies, Parsons said.

“There’s work to do here, but because we’re timing ourselves now, we are actually orienting operations around trying to move those things more quickly,” he said.

The strategy seems to be paying off: DOB’s collection rate for fines increased by 10% from fiscal years 2024 to 2025. Last year, fines collected before final order exceeded $1 million for the first time.

“We’re doing more outreach. We're doing more talking to people. These options have usually been here, but we’re emphasizing them more,” Parsons said. “If you fix [violations] soon enough, we will just resolve it without fines at all.”

Not everyone thinks that’s a win. Browder worries that landlords, some of whom already don’t take the abatement process seriously, won’t be incentivized to make fixes.

“For me it’s really concerning,” she told NOTUS. “I think it just lessens the accountability for landlords to say ‘Hey, you can kind of just limp along and settle with DOB without any meaningful corrective action.’”

Browder thinks informal settlements could be beneficial for smaller landlords, but that bigger housing providers — especially corporate landlords who own multiple properties under LLCs — should be forced to go through the fine collection process. She is hoping for a more transparent violations dashboard, and a public list of the owners of properties held under LLCs.

“DOB enforcement should be the last step before litigation. The landlord should just fix the issue; it shouldn’t get to the point where you have to request DOB,” she said. “If we could figure out who the repeat violators [are], DOB could focus on those folks.”
entries.author: Zara Norman

entries.title: How Lindsey Graham and Mark Sanford’s Friendship Defined 30 Years of Republican Politics
entries.summary: Once close friends, the South Carolinians’ paths chart the Republican Party’s evolution.
entries.content:
No relationship better tells the story of the modern Republican Party than that of Mark Sanford and Lindsey Graham.

The former governor of South Carolina and the late senator were once as close as two politicians could be. But like so many political alignments — and friendships — over the last decade, disagreements over President Donald Trump were too great to overcome.

Eight years ago, Graham said turning against Trump was the reason Sanford had been cast aside in the 2018 primary for his Charleston-area House district, despite nearly a quarter-century of ideologically consistent conservatism.

“What happened here? I think for the first time, Mark misread the tea leaves, and being in for a while became a liability. So he's on the wrong side of new versus old,” Graham told me at the time.

Two days after his defeat, Sanford called it “a Faustian bargain that's going on right now.”

“I'll pander to you if you pander to me,” he said of Trump.

Sanford declined to say whether he included his friend Graham in that bargain.

The two entered the House together in 1995 as part of the Newt Gingrich-led Republican revolution, giving the GOP a majority for the first time in 40 years. They were rabble-rousers back then, and in the years to come, Sanford seemed made in a conservative laboratory for a presidential ticket. Graham evolved into a type of bipartisan wheeler-dealer that’s now a dying breed in the Republican Party.

In a twist of fate that stretches from the Appalachian Trail to Argentina, it was Graham who received the equivalent of a state funeral this week, first with a service inside the Capitol Rotunda and then with Trump as the main eulogist at the National Cathedral.

And it was Sanford who, a few days earlier, stood alone in his backyard, filming a video to launch a long-shot bid to get back to Congress. He’s one of many Republicans trying to win the nomination to replace Graham.

“Lindsey’s death is a reminder to all of us how short and precious life is,” Sanford said in his less-than-two-minute video.
Lindsey Graham (4054x2703, AR: 1.50)He cited his father’s death from Lou Gerhig’s disease, his status as a grandfather and his wish to finally tackle the national debt and shrink the size of federal government — the issues that launched the duo onto the national scene in 1994 — among his reasons for running.

He never mentioned that he and Graham were once so close the late senator was godfather to Sanford’s youngest child.

And he never mentioned that Trump, who supported Sanford’s primary opponent in 2018, has endorsed Graham’s sister, Darline, who is now serving as interim senator.

Sanford attended Wednesday's service for Graham in South Carolina, but he was not among the more than dozen politicians, TV personalities and conservative activists asked to speak at memorial events over two days.

While he declined NOTUS’ interview requests this week, Sanford has tried to paint his rise, fall, rise and fall in politics as a selling point to South Carolina Republicans in this snap primary to be settled in just a couple weeks.
Mark Sanford (4131x2754, AR: 1.50)“All of the ups and downs and what not that I’ve had in life — that all of us have had in life — give us a little bit more humility, give us a little bit more empathy, give us a little bit better perspective, I think, in later chapters in life,” he told a local TV news interviewer on Monday.

The two were more aligned than not in those earlier chapters. Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) let out a solid 10 seconds of laughter when asked Wednesday about his early memories of Graham and Sanford.

“Two of the most colorful members of our class,” said Wicker, who served as master of ceremonies two years ago for the class of 1994 reunion in the Capitol’s Statuary Hall.

In 1997, Graham played a leading role in an attempt to throw Gingrich out as speaker, with support from Sanford and other Republican rebels.

During the 2000 campaign, while their state’s senior Republican leadership lined up behind Texas Gov. George W. Bush, Graham and Sanford signed on with Sen. John McCain’s team.

They traveled their state in McCain’s Straight Talk Express bus and warmed up the crowds for the Arizona senator, who sometimes called them his “running mates,” already knowing their ambitions.

Two years later, Sanford won the governor’s race and Graham won his Senate seat, launching them higher into national politics.
GRAHAM MCCAIN (2956x1970, AR: 1.50)When McCain clinched the 2008 nomination, punctuated by a big win in South Carolina, Graham stood at his side. Sanford remained neutral in that presidential primary, perhaps a sign that his conservative politics diverged from that of Graham and McCain.

Then suddenly, it seemed Sanford’s political career was over. His affair with an Argentinian woman became public in June 2009 after he had gone missing for days and aides gave false assertions he was hiking the Appalachian Trail when he was actually in Buenos Aires.

Many Republicans called for his resignation, and state legislators began impeachment proceedings. But one friend gave him as much support as could be expected.

“I know Mark wants to reconcile with his family. I hope and pray that is possible,” Graham said in a statement that avoided a call for resignation. “Second chances in life are not guaranteed or required. But if they are afforded they can be a real blessing.”

While Jenny Sanford did leave her husband, Graham remained loyal to his friend. In 2013, he rallied support for Sanford during a special election for the House and helped him win back that seat.

It wasn’t Sanford’s messy personal life that ended his relationship with Graham. In the end, the Republican Party they both were a part of had shifted. It was less about conservative ideology and more about being in good company with Trump.

Graham saw the reality and moved with it.
Trump (4274x2849, AR: 1.50)
“Along comes Trump: ‘I'm gonna burn the whole place down.’ I actually can relate to that because that's where I used to be,” Graham told me in that June 2018 interview.

Trump won’t attack critics who he thinks want to “add value” to his success, traditional conservatism be damned, Graham said. “The head of our party is the least ideological person in the history of the Republican Party.”

Graham’s longtime bond with Sanford couldn’t protect the anti-Trump Republican from Trump’s fury during his losing 2018 primary. Graham said he learned from McCain that bygones should be bygones in politics, having gone from being prisoner of war in Vietnam to dealing with that government as a senator, and working with President Barack Obama despite his loss to him in 2008. And instead of fighting against Trump’s takeover of the party, Graham jumped on board.

“So one thing I've learned from John is, when it's over, it's over,” Graham said then.

Graham still held out hope for Sanford’s fourth act in politics if he figured out how to repair things with Trump. But with Sanford, it was never over.
AP331347709959 copy.jpg (4797x3198, AR: 1.50)Sanford launched a brief run in the 2020 Republican presidential primary. This spring, he considered running for the House seat that Republican Rep. Nancy Mace is vacating after her failed bid for governor. Then, he announced he would start a foundation dedicated to taming the national debt. And now, he’s running for Graham’s seat.

Sanford remains an anti-Trump Republican, preaching to a smaller and smaller choir but still hopeful that his decades of experience can win enough support.

He thinks that South Carolina’s voters want a truly competitive primary and will want to know more about Sen. Darline Graham’s views on policy, particularly the debt.

“I don’t think they like this idea of a coronation,” he said in a local TV interview this week.

But even after his last act in politics appeared closed back in June 2018, Sanford was not shutting the door on another comeback.

“Believe me, if there's anybody who ever learned you never say never, it's me,” he told me then.
entries.author: Paul Kane

entries.title: Democrats Mobilize Over Fears Trump Will Deploy Troops to Polls
entries.summary: With a deep partisan split on election security, senators turn to tabletop exercises, encouraging early voting and more.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump hasn’t ruled out deploying troops or federal agents to polling places in November. Democrats are preparing for how to respond in case that happens.

Democratic lawmakers, wary of various potential disruptions to the midterm elections, conducted closed-door tabletop exercises last week that included the possibility of armed federal personnel dispatched near polling places.

Sen. Alex Padilla (D-California), who participated in the exercises led by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, said Democrats are preparing to challenge the administration over any “pretext they would make for this type of deployment — because they would be lies — before those deployments even happen.”

The comments reflect an atmosphere of distrust and a sharp partisan split on election security ahead of a midterm election that will determine which party controls the House and Senate — as the Trump administration has pushed aggressively on election system overhauls.

Democrats have planned for their own Senate election observer program, coordination with local officials and voting rights advocates, and rapid-response legal planning.

They’ve also introduced measures to prevent election interference, although such legislation has almost no chance of becoming law before the midterm elections.

Padilla, who is helping lead the Senate Democrats’ Election Protection Task Force, introduced an anti-election interference bill last week that extends the statute of limitations to prosecute election interference by “troops” and “armed forces.”

He said his effort is informed in part by Trump’s deployment of federalized troops to Los Angeles last year, which tested the limits of how military forces can be used domestically alongside federal law enforcement.

“The deployment was unlawful, and the courts ruled that over time,” Padilla said in an interview. “The legal precedent is set, but Donald Trump disregards the rule of law far too often, so we'll have to be prepared, no matter what.”

The 150-year-old Posse Comitatus Act generally bars military personnel from performing domestic law enforcement, and federal law makes it a crime punishable by up to five years in prison to deploy “any troops or armed men” to any location where voting is taking place. There is a narrow exception if troops are needed to protect voters or respond to an armed threat — which some Democrats fear Trump could claim.

Senate Democrats plan to use election observers at the polls to monitor and document any inappropriate activity so they can respond in the moment and inform potential action by Congress. In the meantime, Padilla said Democrats are encouraging early voting.

“If you cast your ballot by mail, you don’t have to worry about federal agents at the polls on Election Day,” Padilla said. “We’re reminding people of those options, but nonetheless standing up for people’s right to vote free of intimidation on Election Day, if that’s their choice.”

The Democratic National Committee filed a lawsuit against the Justice Department, Pentagon and Department of Homeland Security seeking any records that reveal whether the agencies have planned deployments of federal agents or troops around polling places, ballot drop boxes or election offices.

A judge has directed the agencies to begin producing records Friday.

In the wake of inquiries from Democrats to those three departments, the Department of Homeland Security has said the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency is not planning an aggressive campaign at voting sites during the midterms. Schumer and 11 Senate Democrats sent a letter this week demanding information about the administration’s possible plans.

Democrats already have pointed to a range of recent actions by Trump to justify their fears. He has pushed federal election directives on states, threatened local election officials with prosecution, sought detailed voter and election-worker records, and tied federal funding to changes in state voting practices.

Trump announced in May that he would launch an "Election Integrity Army" and did not rule out sending National Guard or ICE to voting locations. In January, he said he regrets not sending the National Guard to seize election equipment during the 2020 election.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) introduced legislation last month that would require the president to get Congress’s approval before deploying uniformed troops or federal law enforcement. When she asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at a hearing in April whether he would deploy troops to polls, he dismissed it as a “gotcha hypothetical.”

Slotkin, who took part in Schumer’s tabletop exercise last week, said participants considered a scenario out of the “authoritarian playbook,” in which a cyberattack, allegations of widespread noncitizen voting or another security incident could be used to justify sending federal forces to polling places.

Having troops or federal agents handle ballots or voting machines could cast doubt on whether the votes remained secure, opening the door to challenges over whether they should be counted.

“What we see, for instance, in Hungary,” Slotkin said, “is a security incident that only federal forces can somehow respond to.”

Slotkin argued that even if troops and agents did not handle voting machines — which could break the chain of custody and call the votes into question — a visible presence could deter people from voting.

“If you tell me that a ton of ICE agents are going to be surrounding polls and that voters have to go run the gauntlet of masked ICE agents, 100% that’s intimidating,” she said.

Republican lawmakers asked by NOTUS to respond to Democratic concerns were largely dismissive, and several on the Senate Armed Services Committee said they had not heard of any such plans from the administration.

“I think the Democrats are fearmongering and trying to create a scenario where people are more concerned than they should be,” said Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri), a former state attorney general. “It’s a political game more than anything.”

Partisan distrust and splintering over election administration predates Trump’s return to office. For decades, House Democrats and Republicans jointly dispatched staff to observe ballot counting in potentially contested elections. But Republicans broke with that tradition in 2024, deploying their own observers during voting instead of participating in the bipartisan effort that takes place during counting.

House Administration Committee Chair Bryan Steil (R-Wisconsin) said he plans to continue that approach this year, citing the 2024 reelection of Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa) by a paper-thin margin.

“What we learned from the race of Mariannette Miller-Meeks was that it would be beneficial to be deployed at the time of the election,” Steil said. “So we began that policy when I became chairman.”

Democrats argue the move reflects the broader erosion of trust over election administration. Rep. Joe Morelle (D-New York), the panel’s ranking member, said Republicans’ abandonment of the joint election observer program “breaks 50 years of tradition and precedent.”

“Honestly, there’s not too many Republicans I trust anymore on election security, on making sure that we're committed to the administration of our elections, and who aren't willing to allow the president to subvert the process,” Morelle said.

Some of the warnings about the potential use of federal forces during the election are coming from a nonpartisan group of former military lawyers. Retired Maj. Gen. Steven Lepper, of the Former Judge Advocates General Working Group, said the organization has held discussions with multiple congressional offices about the threat and possible legislative safeguards.

But Lepper said that with congressional action to restrict the use of troops at polling places unlikely before the election, the decision to carry out an order to deploy in the midst of an election would ultimately fall on military commanders.

“The unwillingness of Congress to do its job has now placed the burden on military members, on military commanders, to have to either stand up to the president and refuse to obey unlawful orders, or obey unlawful orders and essentially put our military in a position where they're committing crimes,” Lepper said. “It’s just a shameful situation for our military to be put in.”
